1578: Jōan 3 (1173): Mongaku forces his petition at Hōjūji-dono and is exiled to Izu.
1579: Jōan 4 (1174), 3rd month: Go-Shirakawa and Kenshunmon-in make a pilgrimage to Itsukushima.

1589: Bunji 2 (1186), 3rd month: Kujō Kanezane becomes Regent; 4th month: Shizuka Gozen dances at Tsurugaoka; the imperial visit to Ōhara.

1591: Bunji 4 (1188): the Senzai Wakashū is presented to the throne.

1626: About this scroll: how to play, what the records mean, historical sources, and deployment.
1627: You are the In, Go-Shirakawa. From your birth in Daiji 2 to your death in Kenkyū 3, the tale runs nine books, with six side books besides. Every choice shifts the values on your Daily Record, the regard of the great houses, and hidden ties of fate. Some options require high enough values before you may take them; others seem ordinary, yet bear fruit a decade or more later.
1628: You may follow history and witness the whole rise and fall of the Taira and Minamoto; or you may open the gates of Shirakawa-kita-dono by night, grant an In-zen at Shishigatani, go west with the Taira, hand the sword of command to Yoshinaka, back Yoshitsune with the In's own troops, or send a secret In-zen to Hiraizumi, and walk toward a wholly different realm. There are sixteen endings in all.
1629: Your progress is saved automatically each time you enter a new book; from the table of books at the front of the scroll you may begin again at any book you have reached. On reaching an ending, you may also “take back that move” and return to your last choice.
1630: Positive means goodwill; negative means enmity.
1632: Still an ordinary sovereign (0–19) → A minor mountain tengu (20–39) → Sōjōbō of Kurama (40–59) → Tarōbō of Mount Atago (60–79) → The Greatest Tengu in Japan (80+).
1633: Everything in the main books rests on historical sources: Kujō Kanezane's Gyokuyō, Jien's Gukanshō, the Azuma Kagami, the Hyōhanki, the Sankaiki, the Kikki, the Hyakurenshō and the Taiki; the war tales Hōgen Monogatari, Heiji Monogatari, The Tale of the Heike and the Genpei Jōsuiki; the Hōjōki; and Go-Shirakawa's own Ryōjin Hishō and Kudenshū. Many famous scenes from the war tales (the sake-jar jest, the flaming-ox stratagem, Benkei's standing death, and others) are literary embellishments, and each is marked as such in the Historical Notes of its book.
1634: The side books and “an imagined line” are the game's own fiction, and are always marked in the Historical Notes with “This is an imagined line.”
1635: The waka, imayō and passages from the tales quoted here are classics eight hundred years old. Names, offices and dates follow the consensus of Japanese historical scholarship; where accounts differ, the more widely accepted one is used and the matter is explained in the Historical Notes.
1636: All portraits, scene images and tengu pictures in the game are taken from old paintings, picture scrolls, ukiyo-e and photographs of statues held on Wikimedia Commons, nearly all in the public domain. Figures with no surviving portrait are represented by a vermilion seal rather than an invented face. Most portraits were painted by later generations (the Tenshi Sekkan Miei dates from the Kamakura to Nanbokuchō periods, the Zenken Kojitsu from the late Edo period), and may not resemble their subjects.
1637: This scroll is a single HTML file and needs no build step. Name the file index.html and drag it onto Netlify's Drop page to put it online; saves are kept locally in your browser.

1639: The interface and text are available in Chinese, Japanese and English, switchable at any time from the top bar; saves work across all three.
